rationale: A wins because it knows where the floor is and does not decorate holes as facts. Its line "Whether the sensors are physically new or were already in the cover and are now unlocked" is exactly the discipline this update needs. B has useful thinking, but "Here the sensors ship in the hardware" and "Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic" turn unknowns into premises. That is how a founder gets a correction instead of coverage.
gaps_in_A: "The health sensors are behind the top subscription tier" is a little sloppy. The update says the features are software-gated, not that the physical sensors themselves are paywalled.

"This bed changes its temperature while you are doing it" needs the trigger mechanics nailed down before pitching. A wisely asks for that proof, but the headline still implies causality the facts do not yet prove.
A underplays sensor accuracy validation. For SpO2, a health reporter will ask what reference device or method Eight Sleep validated against, not just what the app language says.
gaps_in_B: "Here the sensors ship in the hardware" invents the crucial subscription fact. The update says the features are software-gated; it does not say the sensors are physically present for non-subscribers.

"Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic" is cute and suspect. Sleep clinics already deal in snoring and oxygen signals, and the update only says a clinic study is ongoing with no results.

"CPAP makers and home sleep-test vendors own the snoring-and-oxygen territory" imports a whole competitive market story not provided in the update. That may be true background, but it is not grounded enough for a blind angle set.

"a privately held company funding or partnering on research" smuggles in funding as a possibility in the journalist-care section. Funding and publication control belong in proof questions until confirmed.
